newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says no tinkering with farm subsidy pact.
newsitem.headline: France says no tinkering with farm subsidy pact.

text.p: France's farm minister called on Sunday for full implementation of world trade rules that justify export subsidies to sell on the world grain market.
"We are applying international accords and what I don't understand is how you can start changing the rules in the middle of a game," Philippe Vasseur told a news conference.
He was responding at an international food fair to U.S. complaints about the renewal of wheat export subsidies from the European Union. France is the EU's leading supplier.
Washington says the EU subsidies, restored in September after a 16-month pause, are unnecessary even though the 1994 world trade agreement signed in Morocco permits their use.
"We want to apply the Marrakesh accord, the whole of the accord and nothing but the accord, in the time agreed," Vasseur said after touring the SIAL fair on Sunday evening.
He said the proper time to adjust the rules was when negotiations for a successor accord began in 1999.
The Uruguay Round agreement commits the EU and Washington to cutting subsidised grain exports by 21 percent in volume and by 36 percent in subsidy spending terms between 1995 and 2001.

Both were allowed to subsidise around 20 million tonnes of wheat sales in the first year of the pact ending in mid-1996. But instead they scratched the subsidies altogether from early 1995 as unexpectedly high prices allowed farmers to compete directly on the world market for the first time in 20 years.
Now that wheat has have tumbled from record prices reached earlier this year, the EU has started subsidising wheat sales again, though with much lower hand-outs than in the past.
Vasseur said the validity of subsidies had been rightly questioned when markets were high -- peaking near $300 a tonne in April 1996 -- but now the situation was mainly reversed.
French wheat is currently worth around $175 per tonne for export compared with U.S. benchmark prices of $160 and Argentine prices of less than $145 a tonne, traders say.
Farm officials attending the fair said there was no clear-cut agreement on what the rules allow countries to do if, as in the past year, they fail to meet their subsidy quotas.
Several European countries, supported by French exporters, argue the unused quota can be rolled forward to the next year as long the final target is reached on time in 2001.
But U.S. officials say this is against the spirit of the Uruguay Round, which was meant to rein in heavy subsidies.
The issue is important for mainly French exporters who want to persuade the EU's executive Commission to go all out for markets to compete with Argentine wheat this year.
Adding last year's unused quota to this year's slightly lower allocation would effectively leave the EU able to export with subsidies more than it actually grow.
The Commission, seeking to save money and iron out patchy trade relations with Washington, has said it will use subsidies as little as possible and will avoid undercutting U.S. wheat.
Moos told Reuters earlier on Sunday that Washington would monitor EU spending and would consider restoring its own subsidies if the EU started discounting aggressively.
